newsitem.title: USA: HP's Platt says HP tuned for FY97 growth.
newsitem.headline: HP's Platt says HP tuned for FY97 growth.

text.p: Hewlett-Packard Co Chief Executive Officer Lewis Platt told an analysts meeting the company has entered its 1997 fiscal year tuned for growth in a fiercely competitive marketplace, analysts said.

While providing no projections on the computer group's performance in the fiscal year that began last month, Platt said the company had demonstrated its ability to hold back expenses when required, such as in its recent fourth quarter.
"I will say that we've refueled and tuned the engine of growth and profitability," one analyst quoted Platt as saying in remarks distributed to analysts at the closed meeting.
"We will continue to be a fierce competitor in an intensely- competitive marketplace," Platt was quoted as saying. "We like to win and we'll do what it takes to continue being a winner."

Repeating a strong theme of Hewlett-Packard's recent history of tight financial control, which has become increasingly rigorous as its mix of products shifts towards lower-priced personal computer products, analysts said Platt stressed that cost management remains a priority in every sector.
He said new initiatives "take place within an environment of disciplined restraint on hiring and expense control."
"As Q4's significant slowdown in expense growth would indicate, when we have asked HP people to put on the brakes, they exercise commendable restraint," he said.
Platt repeated that the 1996 fiscal year, in which second half results proved disappointing, was a period of positioning the company and "refueling the HP growth engine."
"We've also been tuning it to achieve maximum performance," Platt told the analysts.
The chief executive said HP has made managing its supply chain a priority and has begun to see payoffs as "just about every business has some reengineering effort in place."

Analysts said the tone of the half-day meeting was restrained, but generally positive, with presentations from HP's treasurer and the heads of its computing operations, the newly-formed Internet group, its printer and personal computing divisions and its research laboratories.

HP management appeared to have acted swiftly to address or fix issues that impacted the second half of fiscal 1996, closing down a disk storage busines that had not been successful and refining its medical products, chemical analysis and test and measurement activities. The company also consolidated marketing activities in its workstation business in Colorado, they noted.

While the workstation business has been weak, analysts said the company has been moving to get applications shifted over to its new products and appeared to be moving the business in a positive direction, despite market weakness.
Bright spots included the company's printing business, where in the Unted States it controls about two thirds of the Inkjet market and three quarters of the LaserJet market.

Favorable trends include as scanning, making multiple copies directly from the desktop across a network and the use of de facto distributed computing in the printing of Web pages locally that have been retrieved across the Internet.

The personal computer lineup is also strong, analysts said, with products ranging from the hand-held Windows CE devices introduced last month to four-way symmetric multi-processing Pentium Pro server products.

HP global PC sales in the first three quarters of calendar 1996 rocketed 55 percent, compared with 18 percent for the overall market, according to International Data Corp, boosting its worldwide market share by one point to 4.5 percent.
HP also discussed new research on technologies that could improve network bandwidth and make networks more secure and robust and even a computer using eyeglasses for a display.
